title: High Temperature Alarm
description: Diagnose and resolve high temperature conditions

n1.text: Temperature is reading high. Let's find out why. Check the cooling fan on the motor or drive enclosure — is it running?
n1.hint: Put your hand near the fan exhaust. You should feel airflow. If the fan is electric, listen for the motor hum.

options.label: Yes, fan is running
options.transition: Fan's running. So the cooling system is working, but it's not enough. Let's check airflow.

options.label: No, fan is stopped
options.transition: There's your problem — no cooling. The equipment is just cooking.

n2.text: Check the air vents and filters. Are they blocked with dust, debris, or anything restricting airflow?
n2.hint: Look at both the intake and exhaust. In dusty environments, filters can clog in a matter of weeks.

options.label: Yes, vents are blocked
options.transition: Restricted airflow — the fan is running but can't move enough air through.

options.label: No, airflow seems OK
options.transition: Airflow is fine. Let's check the load.

n3.text: Is the equipment running at a higher load than usual? More product, higher speed, or heavier items than normal?
n3.hint: More load = more heat generation. If the process has changed recently, that could explain the temperature rise.

options.label: Yes, higher than normal
options.transition: Higher load means more heat. The cooling system may not be sized for this duty.

options.label: No, normal operation
options.transition: Normal load but overheating — something else is going on.

n4.text: Check the ambient temperature around the equipment. Is it unusually hot in the area? Direct sunlight, nearby heat sources, or HVAC issues?
n4.hint: Equipment is rated for a max ambient — usually 40C (104F). If the plant is hotter than that, everything runs warmer.

options.label: Yes, it's hotter than usual
options.transition: High ambient is pushing the equipment over its thermal limit.

options.label: No, ambient seems normal
options.transition: Ambient is fine, load is normal, cooling is working. This needs deeper investigation.

n_fan.text: The cooling fan is dead. Without active cooling, the temperature will keep climbing until something trips or fails.
steps: Reduce the load or stop the equipment to prevent thermal damage
Check the fan motor — is it getting power?
Check for a tripped breaker or blown fuse on the fan circuit
If the fan motor is burned out, replace it
Don't run the equipment without cooling — it'll damage VFD components or motor insulation

n_blocked.text: Blocked vents are choking the cooling. Easy fix — clean them out.
steps: Stop the equipment or reduce load while cleaning
Use compressed air to blow out the filters and vents (blow from inside out)
If filters are disposable, replace them
Clean the fan blades if they're caked with dust
Set a PM schedule to clean filters regularly — every 30 days in dusty environments

n_load.text: The equipment is running hotter because the load has increased. You have a few options.
steps: Reduce throughput or speed to bring temperature back into range
If the higher load is the new normal, the cooling system needs to be upgraded
Check motor current — overcurrent and overtemperature often go hand in hand
Consider adding supplemental cooling (external fan, duct to enclosure)
Monitor temperature trend after load adjustment

n_ambient.text: High ambient temperature is the root cause. The equipment can't reject enough heat when the surroundings are too hot.
steps: Improve ventilation in the area if possible — open doors, add fans
Check if HVAC to this area is working properly
Consider adding a panel air conditioner if this is a recurring issue
Reduce equipment load during peak heat times
Shield the equipment from direct sunlight if applicable

n_investigate.text: Temperature is high but the usual suspects check out. This needs a closer look at the temperature sensor itself and the heat generation source.
steps: Verify the temperature reading with an IR thermometer or contact probe
If the sensor reads high but the equipment feels normal, the sensor may be faulty
Check for bearing wear (generates friction heat)
Inspect drive belts for slippage (friction heat)
If temperature is genuinely high with no obvious cause, schedule a thermographic survey
